t: Listen to a talk in a biology class.
Today I want to look at camouflage, and I'll describe three different strategies, because students often mix them up.
Here, an animal's color simply matches its surroundings.
The snowshoe hare is a nice example.
Its coat is brown in summer, but it turns white in winter, so it matches the snow.
The second strategy is called disruptive coloration.
These animals don't match the background at all.
Instead, they have bold patterns, like stripes or spots, that break up the outline of the body.
A zebra's stripes are the classic case.
When zebras stand together, a predator has trouble seeing where one animal ends and the next begins.
In mimicry, a harmless animal looks like a dangerous one.
For instance, the hoverfly has yellow and black bands, so birds mistake it for a wasp and leave it alone, even though the hoverfly can't sting at all.
So, matching, breaking up the outline, and imitating something dangerous.
